rows.title: smnotland  selfmutant.py never verifies the mutation LANDED in the tree it compiled -- the missing postcondition behind all three recorded hazards

entries.note: MEASURED: a subject outside the mirrored src/ passes the anchor check, lands in NEITHER arm, and the helper prints 'mutant applied but the detector did NOT report a failure' -- both halves false. This UNIFIES the three separately-recorded extra-flags hazards (omitted flags that fail to link; flags making both arms consistently wrong; an absolute path compiling the pristine subject into both arms) as instances of ONE missing postcondition. Fix: after link_tree, require tree/<subject> to be a regular non-symlink file containing `new` exactly once in the mutant arm and `old` exactly once in the pristine arm. Also covers the DrvFs case-slip variant.

*** THE SEAT THAT BUILT THE ANSWER. ***  It CONSTRUCTED THREE ESCAPES and measured each against both the shipped helper and my proposed fix. E1 `old == new` -- a two-file copy, ZERO characters of difference -- is the smallest apparatus failure there is and produced the identical false sentence. E2 `new` = `old` + a trailing comment: lands, compiles, inert. E3 EXTRA_FLAGS naming the subject by ABSOLUTE path: the mutant text DOES land in the tree, so no tree-file postcondition can see it -- and gate_offline.sh:955-963 already calls that 'the dangerous one of the three', which makes the filing's 'unifies the three extra-flags hazards' claim MEASURABLY FALSE. Its answer: compare what the COMPILER PRODUCED, not what the harness wrote -- mutant differs from pristine 12/12, the three escapes byte-identical, 0.048 ms of sha256 against a 1370 ms build. *** AND IT FOUND THE ONE THING THAT WOULD HAVE SHIPPED A VACUOUS CONTROL: with -g or -g3 the PRISTINE arm's binary DIFFERS FROM ITSELF across two tree paths, so binary identity would silently stop firing rather than go red. Re-measured here and confirmed exactly -- and the remedy (build both arms at ONE path) verified: -g3 pristine-vs-pristine IDENTICAL, mutant still differs. *** It derived the timeouts from measurement (slowest build 1.37 s, slowest run 0.31 s), measured the process-group kill (child pgid 32 vs the gate's 11, so killpg provably cannot reach the gate), found three MORE no-token paths, and BUILT A WORKING PROTOTYPE it validated at 12/12.

FLAGSHIP RECORDS AND DOCTRINE SEAT. Badge s. *** IT RULED AGAINST THE ROUND'S OWN SCOPE and the ruling was accepted: *** applying the reopening rule prong by prong, smhang needs a WALL-CLOCK ORACLE, so the 'same detector, no new oracle' prong fails objectively -- and the ledger's grouping argument ('both fixes are a dozen lines together') is a SIZE argument, which is not one of the rule's prongs. It also named a real doctrine gap: the reopening rule was written for emulator sites and it is undecided whether it governs apparatus rounds at all. On the witness ladder it ruled that none of the four values fits an apparatus round and proposed extending the vocabulary today while the ladder is still forward-only. It found TWO WRONG RECORDS IN MY OWN BRIEF -- a '9-line block replaced by a 1-line body' pair that DOES NOT EXIST (the largest is diskimage_io, 4 lines -> 2; my number came from a scratchpad mutant), and a 'verbatim' source quote that had silently dropped the `try:` and so hid the finally/rmtree path the timeout design depends on. Both corrected in the brief. It independently confirmed diskimage_io breaks the fragment count, and VERIFIED selfcheckman is already fixed by 7e3b120. *** ONE CALL OVERTURNED BY MEASUREMENT: it predicted run(timeout=)'s post-kill DRAIN would block forever on the grandchild's pipe. False on POSIX -- CPython calls process.wait() there, not communicate(). Its CONCLUSION survived anyway, for a different reason: run() leaves TWO ORPHANS spinning where killpg leaves zero. ***

46 KB, and it found a hazard NOBODY ELSE DID: a harness in a symlinked SUBDIRECTORY of regress/. link_tree symlinks any directory not containing real_file, and the kernel resolves `sub/../../src/...` by following `sub` FIRST, landing outside the tree. MEASURED here after correcting my own first probe (which copied the flat harness unchanged, so `../src` resolved nowhere -- a SETUP that proved nothing): the tree copy carried the MUTANT marker, what gcc read carried 0, and the binary said RTC_RANGE_PASS. *** AND IT SHOWED THE PANEL'S OWN FIX WOULD MISS IT: gcc records the dep path AS WRITTEN, so a textual dep-list check accepts `sub/../../src/...` as the tree's subject; the assertion must compare realpath. No seat stated that. *** LATENT, not live -- every harness is a flat regress/diff_*.c today. It converged unprompted on whole-file equality and on mirroring directories for real. It also raised a DATA-LOSS path: io_write opens with 'w', which follows symlinks, so a case-colliding entry could truncate the REPO subject. CHECKED and latent only: no case-colliding names exist in any mirrored directory and /tmp is ext4 and CASE-SENSITIVE (tested, not assumed).

rows.title: es438  #438 the FIX round for dev_luna88k.c:816 -- store-as-is, per-CPU latch

entries.note:
FLAGSHIP REVIEW of the shipped rounds. Badge `s`. It re-derived every claim from the repo rather than accepting the ledger, and ran no gates or builds.
* *** IT FOUND gate_hygiene LATENTLY RED AT HEAD -- MEASURED by recomputing that gate's own probe_code() census read-only. *** cf4b083 added luna_intmask_probe.py carrying all three pinned #392 constructs and did NOT move EXPECT_CONVERTED from 16. Confirmed by running gate 6: log-hygiene FAIL, 3 of 48. The commit ran gate 2 and the float selftest; GATE 6 NEVER FIRED. It would have failed the Aug 22 weekly battery as a hygiene regression with a bookkeeping cause -- the phantom-regression class.
* AND THE ROOT CAUSE WAS THAT THE PROBE SHIPPED UNWIRED, so nothing forced a gate run. Its structural point, now in the gate's annotation: a probe that ships WITH its wiring cannot skip the pin. Wiring it into gate 11 immediately proved that twice -- the run found the hygiene red AND that build/'s BINARY was four hours stale (source 18:08 with the fix, binary 13:58 without it), so any measurement against that tree since would have been of the wrong code. The probe reported PRE_FIX_SYMPTOM rather than a confusing failure, which is a detector giving a legible answer when its input is wrong.
* THE THIRD TIME THIS GATE WENT RED FOR THIS REASON, and the second was ONE COMMIT EARLIER THE SAME DAY: the footbridge probe had the identical coupling, a subagent warned about it, it was handled correctly, the annotation recording the lesson was written -- and then the same mistake was made with a different probe. Reading a lesson is not having it.
* *** THE ROUND HAD NO LEDGER ROW AT ALL, and its structural point is the sharpest of the review: A ROUND WITHOUT A ROW IS INVISIBLE TO SECTION H -- the dead-man-switch shape one level up. *** The gate that verifies every stage ran a full panel cannot see a round that never got a row. This row exists because of that finding.
* Q1 THE WITNESS IS GENUINELY RUNG 3, all three clauses, no laundering: committed rig image under R:, no device_add, no new machine; every planted word disassembled and text-compared before stepping, with an encoding mismatch exiting as SETUP rather than passing -- the hand-assembled-encoding trap is guarded. Two controls per the footbridge lesson. Honest limit: it could not re-run the pre-fix arm without building a pre-fix binary, so clause (i) is READ from the operator record.
* Q2 THE SHIPPED COMMENT IS HONEST about the distinction -- every factual claim in it survived checking, and it expressly refutes the over-broad form.
* Q3 THE SEQUENCING INVERSION DAMAGES THE PROCESS RECORD ONLY, NOT THE EVIDENCE, said plainly: clause (i)'s content is order-independent, and there is no mechanism to 'fit' a probe so a one-branch fix removes an unrelated death. What is forfeited is the LICENSING semantics -- the reproduction was meant to license the edit and instead verified it retroactively.
* TWO HARDENING NITS: the PRE_FIX_SYMPTOM verdict does not require C2 to have PASSED, so 'died for the right reason' is enforced by transcript reading rather than by the token -- one `if fails:` guard makes it self-guarding. And Q4: the fuse-write filing is the right call but was filed in a COMMIT MESSAGE ONLY, which by this project's history is how work is forgotten.

dev_vr41xx.c:606 is `int hz = RTCL1_L_HZ / idata` -- an INTEGER divide with RTCL1_L_HZ = 0x8000. The entire domain idata >= 32769 collapses to hz = 0, which timer_clamp_freq then floors SILENTLY to 1e-8 Hz: one tick per 3.17 years. *** A GUEST ASKING FOR 0.5 Hz GETS A TIMER THAT NEVER FIRES. ***  Not 'lands below the floor' -- destroyed BEFORE timer.c ever sees it. Flooring 0 -> 1e-8 in timer.c is CORRECT; a floor complaint there would make this noisier while still wrong.

RUNG-3 WITNESS BUILT TODAY, two subtypes, unmodified in-tree machine, no device_add, every planted word disassembled and text-compared before stepping:
    hpcmips/z50 (VR4121) cold debugger, no boot
    LIVENESS  idata=0x00008000 -> [ vr41xx: rtc interrupts at 1 Hz ]   control green
    SUBJECT   idata=0x00010000 -> [ vr41xx: rtc interrupts at 0 Hz ]   guest asked 0.5 Hz
Identical on mobilepro770. Both required controls present: liveness AND device signature ((vr41xx@0xb000000)+0xd0 plus the device's own message -- RAM produces no line at all). The encoding guard earned its keep: the first run REFUSED a verdict because the expected mnemonic strings were wrong, and reported SETUP rather than passing.

TWO OTHER LEGS MEASURED, one FALSE: *** footbridge is REFUTED *** -- bounded below by emulated_hz / 2^32, so emulated_hz would have to be < 42.95 Hz; on a 33 MHz machine the worst case is 0.0077 Hz, six orders of magnitude above the floor. The jazz leg is much weaker than filed: 64-bit store only (any 32-bit store bottoms out at 2.33e-7 Hz, 23x above floor).

THE OTHER HALF OF THE SAME DEFECT, WHICH DOES MERGE: dev_vr41xx.c:614 `case 0xd2: /* RTCL1_H_REG_W */ break;` is a NO-OP. vr_rtcreg.h:87-88 names RTCL1_L/H_REG_W as the halves of a 32-bit reload, so the high half is silently discarded -- and since L is 16 bits, THE SUB-1-Hz DOMAIN IS EXACTLY THE DOMAIN THAT NEEDS H. Same device, same class, same oracle, one fix design.

Does NOT merge with n4/#429 despite both being 'a guest rate narrowed': different device, OPPOSITE END of the domain, different mechanism (wide-domain ceiling vs integer-division floor collapse), new oracle.

rows.title: floodclass  Guest-drivable host-log floods are a CLASS, not the three instances filed so far -- 72 device files carry fatal() with no latch idiom at all
rows.hold: Instrument shipped; the FIX is a policy question (which paths are genuinely guest-drivable) that needs a panel, not a sweep.

entries.note:
FOUND BY CHECKING A SEAT'S REFRAMING RATHER THAN ACCEPTING IT, and the truth was wider than either version. A panel seat argued that `rtcflood` is a REGRESSION INTRODUCED BY #429 -- 'before #429 there was no fatal() at dev_rtc.c:132, so there was no flood'. MEASURED: dev_rtc.c carried TWO fatal() calls before #429 (863d238) and THREE after, so #429 did add one -- but the other two sit in that same file's unimplemented-access `default:` arm and are EQUALLY UNLATCHED AND EQUALLY GUEST-DRIVABLE. So rtcflood is not a regression; it is a THIRD INSTANCE in a file that already had two, and the seat's framing and the original filing were both narrower than the truth.

That is the same shape as `wdcflood`, filed separately for a different device. So the project's own rule applied late: GREP FOR THE SIBLINGS before filing a third one-line latch. CENSUS, shipped as tools/pipeline/census_floods.py: **84 files under src/devices/ contain fatal(), 776 calls in total, and 72 of those files carry NO LATCH IDIOM AT ALL, holding 543 calls.**

*** THE LIMITS ARE PART OF THE FINDING AND ARE PRINTED ON EVERY RUN. *** The latch column is per FILE, not per PATH -- dev_wdc.c shows two latches and still has the unlatched path wdcflood names -- so 'no latch idiom' is a FLOOR on where to look, never a count of defects. And the tool does NO reachability analysis: most fatal() calls are init-time or genuinely once-only and no guest can drive them. Doing reachability needs the call graph, and a tool that guessed would be worse than one that declines. So 776 and 543 are bounds, not bugs.

WHY IT IS AN INSTRUMENT AND NOT A NUMBER: this project already learned that a count in a commit message goes stale the same week, which is why census_exits.py shipped as a tool. Same contract here. Deliberately NOT wired into precommit: the baseline is large, and freezing it is a POLICY decision rather than a measurement.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE TWO OPEN ROWS: rtcflood and wdcflood should be re-read as instances of this class. Fixing them one at a time is what #265/#269 and #337 already did -- #337 latched three paths in dev_wdc.c and still missed the one wdcflood names, which is the strongest available argument that instance-at-a-time is not working.

entries.ev: src/core/debugmsg.c (debug() vs fatal(), read side by side)

entries.note:
*** WORSE THAN FILED, ON TWO MEASUREMENTS -- AND ONE OF THEM REFUTES A CLAIM IN THE TOOL I SHIPPED FOR THIS ROW. ***

(1) THE EMIT PATH AMPLIFIES 161x, MEASURED. va_debug() (debugmsg.c:118-137) emits ONE printf("%c") PER CHARACTER, plus an indent loop printing spaces one at a time. The seat replicated that loop byte-for-byte rather than paraphrasing it and benchmarked against a single fputs, to /dev/null so sink cost is excluded: 0.490 s vs 0.003 s over 200,000 calls on a 62-byte message -- 2.45 us against 0.02 us, AMPLIFICATION 161.2x, and that is a FLOOR because a real line-buffered console is worse. So a flood is not log noise; it is guest-controlled HOST-CPU amplification on a path -q cannot silence.

(2) *** census_floods.py SAYS REACHABILITY 'NEEDS THE CALL GRAPH, AND A TOOL THAT GUESSED WOULD BE WORSE THAN ONE THAT DECLINES'. THAT PREMISE IS FALSE AND I WROTE IT. ***  DEVICE_ACCESS() IS the dispatch entry memory_rw calls, so lexical containment inside its brace-matched body is a SOUND STRUCTURAL OVER-APPROXIMATION -- no call graph required. The seat built it:
    776 fatal() under src/devices/
    475 inside a DEVICE_ACCESS() body            (guest MMIO handler)
    150 inside a switch default: in that body    (unhandled-offset arm)
     10 of those guarded by a latch in their OWN arm
    *** 140 UNLATCHED AT THE SITE, in 53 files ***
POSITIVE CONTROLS BOTH LAND, and it resolves PER-PATH -- the resolution my census says it lacks. It flags dev_rtc.c:168-173 (the two pre-#429 arms this row names), and in dev_wdc.c it correctly SEPARATES :731/:761 (latched by warned_badlen, #337's work) from :583/:1007 (unlatched) -- i.e. it finds the path #337 MISSED inside a file my census scores as 'latched'.

SO THE HONEST HEADLINE IS 140 SITES, NOT 543 CALLS AND NOT 72 FILES. Per-path, actionable, and mechanically re-derivable.

(3) A RUNG-3 WITNESS IS AVAILABLE TODAY AT NEAR-ZERO COST, and the filing seat (me) missed it: regress/pit8253_latch_probe.py is committed and already drives real guest ARM instructions through real address decode to PA 0x7c000040-43 on an unmodified -E cats -- the 8253's own registers -- and dev_8253.c carries unlatched default:-arm fatal() at :158 and :184 (plus :250/:253). ONE MORE ARM on an already-committed probe witnesses an unsuppressable 161x-amplified flood.

(4) DETECTOR, NOT FIX, AND THE REASON IS STRUCTURAL: the round-scope rule takes ONE site, and a second only in the SAME DEVICE. rtcflood and wdcflood are different devices, so THE PROJECT'S OWN SCOPE RULE FORBIDS FIXING THIS CLASS IN ONE ROUND -- 140 sites at one round each is not a plan. What a floodclass round can honestly deliver is the per-path detector plus the ranked list.

HONEST BOUND THE SEAT INSISTED ON, and it is right: the harm is to the HOST (CPU burn, unbounded log growth, unsuppressable), NOT to the emulated guest. floodclass is a host-side denial-of-service surface, not guest corruption. It still outranks the rest of its cluster because the others have no harm of any kind -- theirs is a wrong record.

rows.title: pitflip  The 8253's 16-bit LSB/MSB selector is one-way, so it manufactures a count of 0 and silently loses bytes
rows.hold: Reachable by an ordinary driver; the measure seat ranks it and pitlatch ABOVE the count-0 item on severity-and-reachability.

entries.note: MEASURED at rung 3. dev_8253.c:170-171 CLEARS I8253_TIMER_LSB and nothing ever sets it back; a real 8254's flip-flop ALTERNATES on every access. Two full LSB/MSB pairs after one mode write produced THREE recomputes -- 97 Hz, **0 Hz**, 97 Hz -- where hardware does two. TWO CONSEQUENCES, and the first is what makes it matter: it transiently drives the counter to ZERO, i.e. straight into the i8253zero defect, FROM A GUEST THAT NEVER PROGRAMS COUNT 0. That inverts the reachability finding on i8253zero, where no available guest asks for count 0 directly. Second: if the second pair's LSB is nonzero it is SILENTLY LOST -- intending 0x3055 the device holds 0x3000. Same device and the same semantic class as i8253zero (counter-load byte routing), so it is the natural companion if a round takes a second site.

agy answered this panel. SECOND in the panel's sequence, and NOT merged with i8253zero despite the measure seat proposing exactly that. It is the row that makes i8253zero reachable at all, which is why it precedes it.

grok answered this panel. SECOND in the panel's sequence, and NOT merged with i8253zero despite the measure seat proposing exactly that. It is the row that makes i8253zero reachable at all, which is why it precedes it.

kimi answered this panel. SECOND in the panel's sequence, and NOT merged with i8253zero despite the measure seat proposing exactly that. It is the row that makes i8253zero reachable at all, which is why it precedes it.

8253/8254 PIT CLUSTER: five MEASURED defects at one site, brought to the panel with the scope question promoted to Q0 -- the brief did not ask whether they are real (a rung-3 reproduction had settled that) but WHICH IS THE ROUND and how many may travel together.

*** Q0 ANSWERED UNANIMOUSLY: NO MERGES. FIVE SEPARATE ROUNDS. ***  agy: 'split pitflip, pitlatch, pitlsb and isaorder into separate candidate rounds'. glm: 'none merge under the one-fix-design test'. deepseek: 'no merges'. minimax sequenced them rather than combining. **This OVERRULES the measure seat's own suggestion that pitflip was 'the natural companion' to i8253zero** -- it argued same-device and same-semantic-class (counter-load byte routing), and the panel applied the remaining prongs and said no. The measuring seat found the defects; the panel scoped them, and the two jobs came apart cleanly.

WHAT IS FIRST -- pitlatch, 3 to 1:
  pitlatch    deepseek, glm, minimax. glm's clause is the decisive one: 'a real guest reaches it in microtime()'. That is this project's ordering rule applied exactly -- severity and reachability, never rung, never vote -- and pitlatch is the only one of the five demonstrated to be on a path a shipped guest actually takes (_guest-src-openbsd22/sys/arch/i386/isa/clock.c:207-209).
  i8253zero   agy alone, as a standalone fix round.
MINIMAX GAVE THE MOST REASONED SEQUENCE and it is worth keeping: pitlatch, then pitflip, then **i8253zero THIRD 'once pitflip closes its door'** -- because pitflip is what MANUFACTURES count 0 from a guest that never asks for it, so fixing pitflip removes i8253zero's main reachability route and lowers its rank. That is a dependency between rounds, not a merge.

*** THE FACT THAT DECIDES WHAT THIS ROUND CAN HONESTLY DO: THERE IS NO RUNNING COUNT. ***  Found while writing the design brief. d->counter[3] is WRITTEN only in the mode-write path and READ only in the counter-read path -- IT NEVER DECREMENTS. timer0_tick() increments pending_interrupts_timer0 and touches nothing else. The file's own header carries the author's TODO at line 35: '(Split counter[] into reset value and current value.)'

So d->counter[] is the PROGRAMMED RELOAD VALUE, FROZEN. gxemul models the timer's RATE (timer_add / timer_update_frequency) and its INTERRUPTS, but never a counting register.

WHY THAT REFRAMES THE FIX: OpenBSD's microtime() latches and reads the counter to INTERPOLATE SUB-TICK TIME. If a 'correct' latch returns a constant, the guest's interpolated time does not advance within a tick -- a different wrong answer from 0, and arguably a WORSE one because it is plausible rather than obviously broken. So the candidate that looks most correct (return the programmed value) may be the one that misleads a guest furthest, and the honest round may be smaller than the row implies: make the latch not-an-error and not-a-flood, and DOCUMENT that sub-tick interpolation is unmodelled. The panel was asked exactly that, and asked to say so if this is a DOCUMENT round wearing a FIX round's clothes.

entries.note:
*** THE DRIVING SEAT REFUSED THE PANEL'S DESIGN AND MEASURED WHY. ***  Four of six seats converged on 'make the latch non-clobbering and non-fatal, RETURN THE RELOAD VALUE, and document that it is not a live count'. The seat BUILT that as candidate C1 and measured it causing a GUEST DIVIDE-BY-ZERO: OpenBSD's findcpuspeed() (_guest-src-openbsd22/.../clock.c:333-344) programs the counter to 0xffff and divides by (0xffff - gettick()); under C1 gettick() returns 0xffff, so the divisor is 0.

AND C1 DID NOT EVEN DELIVER WHAT IT PROMISED: it returned the HIGH BYTE TWICE (0x2e2e, not the reload 0x2e9c), because pitflip leaves the LSB/MSB selector stuck at MSB. The 'return the reload value' option does not return the reload value.

*** THE SEAT-CLASS DOCTRINE DECIDED IT, NOT THE COUNT. ***  The three seats voting for the reload value were the PACKET-FED Ollama seats, which PIPELINE.md says are never equivalent votes on repo fact. Verified in source: latched[] is SET at :212, cleared ONLY at :219 by a non-latch mode write, and NEVER cleared by the read at :163. The seat that had been WALLED for the pass-1 panel is the one that found it, which is the clearest argument this campaign has produced for discharging a wall rather than recording it and moving on. glm gestured at the same thing ('the sticky latch').

MEASURED (build/gxemul, -v -v -V -T -E cats -M 32): device order is 8259 @0x7c000020, 8259 @0x7c0000a0, *** 8253 @0x7c000040 ADDED AFTER BOTH PICs, *** pccmos @0x7c000070. The pointer copy sits at bus_isa.c:224-225, between the first device_add (:223) and the second (:235); the 8253's device_add is at :244. Construction order confirmed in the RUNNING PROGRAM, not inferred -- and it independently confirms the 0x7c000040 mapping.

MEASURED (grep census): pending_timer_interrupts has exactly ONE writer (dev_8253.c:282) and TWO pointer-cachers (bus_isa.c:225, dev_v3.c:298), both caching before their 8253 can exist.

*** MEASURED, AND THIS IS THE PART NOBODY STATED: dev_8253.c contains ZERO decrements of pending_interrupts_timer0. ***  Every other timer device in the tree drains its own counter from inside its own DEVICE_ACCESS handler -- dev_jazz.c:423,443, dev_luna88k.c:800, dev_mc146818.c:563, dev_vr41xx.c:634, dev_footbridge.c:583,594-595. The 8253 ALONE outsourced its drain to bus_isa.c:134-138.

READ: that drain is unreachable for TWO INDEPENDENT reasons, *** so moving the pointer copy after device_add -- the fix as filed -- changes NOTHING observable: *** (1) nothing ever calls isa_interrupt_deassert for line 0, as dev_8253.c has no INTERRUPT_DEASSERT; and (2) dev_8259.c clears irr DIRECTLY on EOI (:107, :122), bypassing the isa deassert handler entirely.

REFILE AS: 'the 8253's pending-interrupt counter has no reachable drain -- it is the only timer device in the tree that cannot ack', grade DESIGN + needs-witness. Consequence (READ): once any guest touches the PIT, in_use goes 1, the counter rises monotonically and never drains, so DEVICE_TICK re-asserts isa.0 on EVERY device tick (TICK_SHIFT 14) rather than at the programmed rate.

TWO THINGS THE FILING SEAT MISSED: dev_v3.c:298 is not merely 'the same shape' -- it is the same bug for the same reason needing the same two-part fix; and if a machine ever created two ISA buses (bus_pci.c calls bus_isa_init at :476 and :1060), the second copy would be NON-NULL AND ALIAS THE FIRST BUS'S 8253 -- worse than NULL, and silent.

THE WITNESS THAT WOULD SETTLE IT, rung 3 on -E cats: program counter 0 to ~18 Hz, free-run 200 ms, read the 8259 IRR (expect bit0), write specific-EOI 0x60 to 0x7c000020, free-run ~5 ms, read IRR again. Draining correctly => 0 (next tick due at ~55 ms); no drain => 1 again on the very next device tick. Clean discriminator, no source change.

entries.note:
*** THE DRIVING SEAT REFUSED THE PANEL'S DESIGN AND MEASURED WHY. ***  Four of six seats converged on 'make the latch non-clobbering and non-fatal, RETURN THE RELOAD VALUE, and document that it is not a live count'. The seat BUILT that as candidate C1 and measured it causing a GUEST DIVIDE-BY-ZERO: OpenBSD's findcpuspeed() (_guest-src-openbsd22/.../clock.c:333-344) programs the counter to 0xffff and divides by (0xffff - gettick()); under C1 gettick() returns 0xffff, so the divisor is 0.

AND C1 DID NOT EVEN DELIVER WHAT IT PROMISED: it returned the HIGH BYTE TWICE (0x2e2e, not the reload 0x2e9c), because pitflip leaves the LSB/MSB selector stuck at MSB. The 'return the reload value' option does not return the reload value.

*** THE SEAT-CLASS DOCTRINE DECIDED IT, NOT THE COUNT. ***  The three seats voting for the reload value were the PACKET-FED Ollama seats, which PIPELINE.md says are never equivalent votes on repo fact. BOTH FILE-READING seats that answered (agy, grok) warned against it, and kimi flagged the same hazard class. Codex was a SEAT FAILURE at that panel, not agreement. A 4-2 count concealed a 0-2 split among the seats that could open the file.

WHAT SHIPPED (#439): the latch is ACCEPTED, latches NOTHING, and disturbs NO state -- a latched[3] flag, a write-arm branch returning before it touches mode_byte/mode[], and a read-arm branch returning 0 with the limitation documented in the code and in the file header. Guest-visible values are unchanged from the committed build, so it cannot regress anything. pitclobber travels with it: one fix design ('the latch disturbs no state') covers both arms.

MEASURED, rung 3, unmodified -E cats, PIT at 0x7c000040, five controls green in every run (RAM liveness, CP15 MMU-off readback, a device signature RAM cannot produce, an MMU-ON negative control, encodings checked against the emulator's own disassembly):
    committed HEAD  mode_byte after latch 0x00 (DESTROYED), latched reads 0x00 0x00,
                    two 'huh? reading from counter 0' complaints
    shipped         mode_byte after latch 0x24 (PRESERVED), 0 complaints,
                    findcpuspeed divisor 65535 (safe)

THE DETECTOR KILLS PER VARIANT, INCLUDING THE OVER-FIX:
                    R1 clobber   R2 false error   R3 divisor
    committed HEAD     FAIL          FAIL            ok
    C1 panel shape      ok            ok            FAIL = 0
    C2 read-arm only   FAIL           ok             ok
    shipped             ok            ok             ok
R3 exists specifically to catch the plausible over-fix the panel recommended.

*** THE SEAT CAUGHT A VACUITY BUG IN ITS OWN FIRST DRAFT: *** the rows read absent registers as ok (-1 == -1), so three 'kills' were runs that never started -- an execvp PATH bug. Rows now fail on absent data (R0), and R0 is why the table above can be believed.

FOUR CLAIMS IN MY BRIEF MEASURED FALSE, and one of them I had propagated all evening: fatal() is NOT 'byte-for-byte debug()' -- debug() returns early under quiet_mode/verbosity and fatal() never does, so a fatal() flood CANNOT BE SILENCED even with -q, which makes every flood row MORE severe. The guest function is gettick(), not microtime(). d->mode[] is behaviourally inert (written in three places, read only inside a debug() printf), so pitclobber's only guest-visible effect is via mode_byte. And 'return the reload value' does not return the reload value.

rows.title: warnnotfail  Deleting a pipeline checker still yields PRECOMMIT_PASS, because the MISSING branches only warn
rows.hold: One-line change per branch, but it is a POLICY decision -- a missing checker in a fresh clone is different from one deleted in a working tree.

entries.note:
MEASURED by a ninth-seat review. precommit_check.sh:45 defines warn () { soft "$@"; } -- so it increments `warn`, not `fail`. Deleting check_witness.py today still yields PRECOMMIT_PASS with a single WARN line.

THE HISTORICAL BUG IS FIXED AND THIS IS THE NEXT LAYER: `warn` was once UNDEFINED, so a deleted checker printed 'warn: command not found' to stderr and its gate vanished in SILENCE. That was corrected earlier this session. Announcing now works; BLOCKING does not -- and the file's own comment says those branches exist 'to announce' the failure, which is exactly as far as they go.

Deliberately filed rather than fixed on the spot: a missing checker in a FRESH CLONE is a normal state, while one deleted from a working tree is a gate being switched off, and the branch cannot currently tell them apart. Making it hard without that distinction would block a clean clone from committing.

The smnotland fix makes an out-of-src subject WORK, including regress/ -- i.e. THE DETECTOR ITSELF. Subject regress/diff_rtc_range.c, anchor = the row's own line, one digit changed in its expected value:

Those three lines map to exactly BE300 (:72), E105 (:102), VR3 (:223). *** THREE BAD SITES, THREE ABORTING SUBTYPES, 1:1. ***  The /* TODO: irq? */ above :114 is the author's own flag. Upstream defect, inherited: git log shows only 39748e3. Identical in est/ and SEC.

Ranked SECOND behind the vr41xx narrowing, deliberately: the silent defect outranks the loud one by this project's own dev_footbridge.c:136-141 reasoning -- a guest waiting forever on a tick that never comes is worse than a loud recoverable fault.

rows.title: sh4bcr  A guest 4-byte store to SH4_BCR2/BCR3 terminates the host process -- rung-3 witnessed, 5/5 controls green, on an unmodified -E landisk
rows.hold: Ranked FIRST of the memory/device-access cluster. Two-site round (BCR2 + BCR3): same device, same class, one fix design, same detector, no new oracle -- measured 5/5.

entries.note:
*** THE SHARPEST WITNESS OF THE SESSION, AND IT IS FILED NOWHERE: *** no BCR2, BCR3 or 'Non-16-bit' appears in OUTSTANDING_BUGS.md, CHANGELOG.md or ledger.json.

MEASURED, stock build/gxemul, unmodified in-tree -E landisk, cold debugger, real SH-4 decode, real memory_rw, real device dispatch. No source edited, no device_add:
    L_liveness_RAM               alive=True  val=efbeadde              ok
    S_device_signature_BCR2      alive=True  val=fd3f0000              ok
    N_neg_ctrl_BCR1_32bit_store  alive=True                            ok
    A_DEFECT_BCR2_32bit_store    alive=False fatalmsg=True  HOST KILLED ok
    A2_DEFECT_BCR3_32bit_store   alive=False fatalmsg=True  HOST KILLED ok
A guest `mov.l r0,@r1` with r1 = 0xff800004 reaches dev_sh4.c:1409, prints 'Non-16-bit SH4_BCR2 access?' and calls exit(1). *** TWO GUEST INSTRUCTIONS, HOST GONE. ***  dev_sh4 is registered unconditionally by cpu_sh.c:200 over SH4_REG_BASE + 0x01000000, so the address is in range; being SH-4 P4 space it needs no MMU setup.

*** THE NEGATIVE CONTROL IS THE SHARP ONE: SH4_BCR1 at 0xff800000 has NO len check at all (:1399), so the same device, the same 4-byte width, FOUR BYTES AWAY, SURVIVES. *** The kill is the width test, not the device. Device signature: writing 0xffff to BCR2 at legal width reads back 0x3ffd = idata & 0x3ffd (:1413) -- RAM would have returned 0xffffffff.

*** AND THIS REFUTES THE hlen CENSUS'S OWN IMMUNITY CLAIM: *** it states 'SH-4 is provably immune', scoped to 8-byte accesses. SH-4 turns out to be the family where the host kill was MEASURED, using a 4-byte access, which SH-4 issues freely. The census's discriminator ('does it mention len') undercounts the class and so does its immunity argument.

FIX SHAPE is the #438 shape: keep the fatal() diagnostic, drop the exit(1), service at the register's natural width. Note the existing regress/sh_halt_probe.py covers cpu->running = 0 halts ONLY, not exit(1), so it is blind to this by construction.

*** THE SMALLEST EDIT THAT BREAKS #429 AND SURVIVES ITS ENTIRE TABLE. ***  MEASURED.

    src/devices/dev_rtc.c:92
    idata = memory_readmax64(cpu, data, len);  ->  idata = memory_readmax64(cpu, data, 4);
On a little-endian guest a 2^32 write yields idata = 0 -> d->hz = 0 -> *** THE ADD BECOMES A REMOVE, *** the exact mechanism diff_rtc_range.c's own header describes. Result: 18 rows, 0 failures, RTC_RANGE_PASS. Invisible because the STUB returns stub_in whole and never looks at len. #427's clamp in timer.c cannot mask it -- the timer is GONE, not clamped.

It came out of a full census over the HZ write path (18 statement deletions + 12 substitutions) which found TEN survivors. The other nine worth naming: `>` -> `>=` (see [[rtcbranch]]); deleting `if (d->timer != NULL)` (:141); deleting `d->timer = NULL` (:144); deleting `d->pending_interrupts = 0` (:145); deleting the `else` at :151; `idata == 0` -> `idata == 1` (a guest asking 1 Hz gets the timer REMOVED -- the 'zero keeps its meaning' rows do not pin that ONLY zero stops it); the 32-bit mask on the pass-through (a true no-op, correct to pass); and timer_add / timer_update_frequency fed raw idata.

THREE STUBS ARE UNFAITHFUL AND EACH HIDES A SURVIVOR: memory_readmax64 ignores len AND cpu (the real one dereferences cpu->byte_order and reads exactly len bytes); timer_remove accepts NULL silently, where the real one (timer.c:155-175) walks to cur == NULL, finds `cur == t` TRUE, then dereferences cur->next -- *** a guaranteed NULL deref that the table survives because no row writes 0 with d.timer == NULL, the ordinary reset path; *** and memory_writemax64 is a no-op with no row doing a MEM_READ, so the guest readback (dev_rtc.c:110) is asserted nowhere.

fatal is faithful in the respect that matters -- debugmsg.c:384 calls va_debug and does not exit -- so pass 3's 'REFUTED BY SOURCE' record is correct.

rows.title: rtcbranch  diff_rtc_range.c:239 claims a `>=` would fail its row; MEASURED, it fails NOTHING
rows.hold: Merges into [[rtclen]]'s detector round -- same file, same oracle, one fix design.

entries.note:
The comment reads 'a >= here would fail this row and nothing else.' MEASURED FALSE: it fails NOTHING. The row 'INT_MAX exactly: passed through, not clamped' prints ok 2147483647 either way, *** because the clamp target EQUALS the boundary -- the clamp is idempotent there. *** The row asserts the VALUE, not which branch ran.

What actually changed was a FOURTH stderr line -- '[ rtc: rate 2147483647 is above the timer domain; clamped ]' -- for a perfectly legal rate. The gate already merges stderr into RTCLOG via 2>&1 and asserts NOTHING about it.

CHEAPEST CLOSURE, in the round's own idiom: the detector already defines its own fatal() -- add `static int fatal_calls;` and assert 0 for the INT_MAX and 1048577 rows, 1 for each out-of-range row. That kills `>=` and gives R7 the branch pin it claims. Free alternative with no C change: check the grep -c of 'is above the timer domain' in RTCLOG equals 3.

rows.title: rtcstale18  Three records say the RTC table has 17 rows; it has 18 -- including the file that cites this exact staleness class as its reason for naming the number
rows.hold: Records-only. Rolls into [[rtclen]]'s round for free.

entries.note:
gate_offline.sh:1161 reads '# Floor 9 -> 12 -> 17' and cites the sh4_tmu incident (*'the comment said 16->17 while the code read 18'*) as its reason for naming the value; :1167 reads 18. af40df5 changed the code only. Same staleness at diff_rtc_range.c:76 ('the 17-row table (17 rows, 0 failures)') and selfmutants/rtc_range.why:11 -- *** the latter INSIDE THE PARAGRAPH THAT FLAGS THIS CLASS. ***

Also in the same sweep: the .why's stated reason for preferring the one-liner anchor ('selfmutant.py requires a UNIQUE anchor and both qualify') is not the discriminator -- the revert fragment is ALSO unique. The second reason given (survives reindentation) is the real one.

The greps are otherwise sound. One note for whoever touches them: every named-row check is a PRESENCE grep matching the FAIL line as well as the ok line, which is safe only because `row failures == 0` is asserted separately.

rows.title: pitcount  The 8253 models no decrementing count, so OpenBSD's delay() never returns -- under every design discussed, INCLUDING the one that shipped
rows.hold: The row with the real guest value, and the one nobody filed. Needs a decrementing count model -- a design item, not a small fix.

rows.title: ledgerboiler  The ledger records that seats were FIRED as though they AGREED -- 52 rows carry one summary stamped across five seat cells
rows.hold: The CHECK ships now, forward-only. Re-harvesting 52 archived rows from the original seat files is a separate and much larger records round -- and may not be worth it: the seat files still exist under _scratchpad/panel_*/, so the archived cells are recoverable rather than lost.

entries.note:
*** A DEFECT IN MY OWN HARVESTING, FOUND BY A REVIEWING SEAT, AND IT IS FIFTY-TWO ROWS RATHER THAN THE ONE IT NAMED. ***

The seat looked at wdcnoirq and found the agy, grok, kimi, deepseek and minimax cells differ ONLY in the leading seat name -- 378/379/379/383/382 bytes of "<seat> answered this cluster panel. ROUND B, with wdcstandby. The seats were clear that...". *** Three of those seats had ARGUED IN THEIR OWN FILES THAT ROUND B WAS TOO NARROW, *** and deepseek's 5.3 KB answer never mentions the 0xF5 opcode at issue at all -- yet the record shows five seats concurring with the narrow scope.

Under the PIPELINE doctrine the ledger is the SINGLE SOURCE OF TRUTH. A harvest that stamps one summary across every seat cell does not merely lose detail: *** it converts 'six seats answered' into 'six seats agreed', which is the exact claim the panel exists to earn. ***  It is the seat-count analogue of the padded-column grep trap -- the number looks right and means nothing.

*** AND THE FIRST CHECK I WROTE TO VERIFY THE CLAIM REPORTED GREEN. ***  It hashed the note text, so a four-character seat-name prefix turned five identical paragraphs into five distinct hashes, and I briefly recorded the seat's finding as measured false. Blindness reported as a green line, in the verification of a finding about blindness being reported as a green line. The shipped check strips the seat's own name before comparing, which is what makes it work.

SCALE, measured: 57 clusters across 52 rows, at >= 3 seats sharing a >= 80-char note. That is essentially every cluster panel ever recorded. So the check is FORWARD-ONLY BY DATE, not by an allowlist -- a per-row allowlist at that scale is the check switched off with extra steps, and a rule that retro-fails the archive gets disabled.

Negative-controlled both directions: injecting three cloned post-cutoff entries gives BOILERPLATE_FAIL naming the row; restoring gives BOILERPLATE_PASS 57 archived, 0 new.

rows.title: wdcoracle  Deleting one line from dev_wdc_tick() leaves a controller that can NEVER raise an interrupt -- and a struct-reading opcode detector stays 100% green
rows.hold: Not a defect round -- a design constraint on the wdcnoirq and wdcflood detectors. Consume it when either ships; there is nothing to fix on its own.

entries.note:
*** THE ANSWER TO 'WHAT IS THE SMALLEST EDIT THAT BREAKS THIS AND STILL PASSES', AND IT INVALIDATES THE DETECTOR DESIGN THE wdcnoirq ROUND WAS ABOUT TO SHIP. ***  MEASURED, both oracles built in one harness.

M1: delete `INTERRUPT_ASSERT(d->irq);` from dev_wdc_tick() (dev_wdc.c:113). ONE LINE.
                     ORACLE A (reads d->int_assert)   ORACLE B (counts real asserts)
    IDENTIFY 0xec        int_assert=1                     irq_asserts=0
    RECAL    0x10        int_assert=1                     irq_asserts=0
    STANDBY  0xe0        int_assert=1                     irq_asserts=0
    HELD-LINE 0x10, 1000 ticks:                           0 asserts
*** Oracle A is 100% green on a controller that can never raise an interrupt, on any machine, for any opcode. ***  The detector's oracle for wdcnoirq is THE WRONG VARIABLE. This is diff_wdc_identify.c's own recorded blind spot one level up ('this driver reads identify_struct DIRECTLY rather than through the path the guest uses').

So the wdcnoirq round's detector must count real INTERRUPT_ASSERT calls through d->irq.interrupt_assert, not read d->int_assert. ~6 lines of harness, not a new gate.

TWO MORE SURVIVORS FROM THE SAME CENSUS:
M3 -- move `d->int_assert = 1;` into wdc_command()'s prologue. Every abort row flips to irq=1 exactly like the real fix, AND *** 0xA0 ATAPI_PKT_CMD flips 0 -> 1, silently re-enabling the interrupt the shipping code DELIBERATELY suppresses at :559 *** (`/* d->int_assert = 1; */`). A 9-row set without an 0xA0 row passes completely. Dangerous because it looks like a tidy-up a later refactor would make. The detector needs an 0xA0 row asserting irq == 0 -- 0xA0 is the file's ONLY deliberate no-interrupt arm and nothing pins it.
M4 -- add `d->warned_unimpl = 0;` to the prologue (the flood latch never latches). Flood back to 100/100, and *** every per-opcode row is byte-identical to the correct post-fix build. ***  Only a repeat-the-same-opcode-ON-THE-SAME-STRUCT row catches it -- so if the detector allocates a fresh wdc_data per row, which is the natural way to write it, THE FLOOD FIX IS UNDETECTABLE.
entries.ev: /tmp/opuswdc/probe.c: Oracle A vs Oracle B, M1/M3/M4

rows.title: stalecopies  Three unpatched pre-#337 copies of dev_wdc.c live under the project root, and a file-reading seat cited one of them as "root"
rows.hold: Owner decision on which fix: retarget --add-dir, delete build-asan/, or amend the brief template. Deleting anything under the project root needs the owner's word.

entries.note:
*** A SEAT-INFRASTRUCTURE TRAP, NOT A HARNESS DEFECT -- BUT IT PRODUCED WRONG LINE CITATIONS IN A PANEL ANSWER THAT WAS OTHERWISE CORRECT. ***  Kimi cited 'root dev_wdc.c:414, :422' and 'root 520-527'. Neither matches GXEMUL-SEC (466, 474, 572-579). find shows THREE unpatched copies under the project root -- ./src/, ./build-asan/src/, ./_archive/... -- all with SEC_SET_PASSWORD@520 and ZERO warned_ references. Kimi read the unhardened upstream and called it 'root'. Its CONCLUSIONS held; its citations did not.

This is live for any file-reading seat given --add-dir at the PROJECT ROOT rather than at GXEMUL-SEC, which is how panel.sh invokes agy. build-asan/ is a June-27 leftover and gate_asan_sweep.sh uses /tmp/gx-asan-head, so nothing depends on it.

The cheap fixes are a choice, not a design: point --add-dir at GXEMUL-SEC; or delete build-asan/; or add a line to the brief template naming the tree the seat must cite. The last is the only one that also covers _archive/, which is deliberately kept.

Recorded because 'the seat cited the wrong tree' is indistinguishable in the output from 'the seat hallucinated a line number', and this project has spent real effort on that distinction before -- see the ARM-manual page-number history in CLAUDE.md.
entries.ev: find for dev_wdc.c under the project root; SEC_SET_PASSWORD@520 vs :572-579
